title: Family, age, and surprising questions
title_target: ครอบครัว — Khrâwp-khrua
goal: Name family members with a system that distinguishes older from younger, say your age, and answer personal questions that in Thailand count as friendly — not nosy.
bekal: name members of your immediate and extended family
use พี่ and น้อง according to age, not gender
ask and give ages with อายุ
answer questions about marital status and children
use พี่/น้อง to address strangers

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Lunch in the cafeteria, showing photos
dialogs.intro: Nok shows a photo of her family. Notice that Thai words for siblings first ask "older or younger", and only then "male or female" — the reverse of English "brother" and "sister".

notes: **Thai divides siblings by AGE first, and only then by gender.** *พี่ phîi* = older sibling, *น้อง náwng* = younger sibling. Then *ชาย chaai* (male) or *สาว sǎao* (female) is added: *พี่ชาย* (older brother), *พี่สาว* (older sister), *น้องชาย* (younger brother), *น้องสาว* (younger sister). English starts with gender (brother/sister) and often leaves age unsaid; Thai can't.

**พี่ and น้อง go far beyond family — they're the social addressing system of the whole country.** An older coworker is called *พี่*, a younger server is *น้อง*, and neighbors, vendors, drivers all fall into one of these two words. That's why Thais need to know your age.

**So asking someone's age in Thailand is NOT rude.** ⚠️ This is the opposite of the habit in many Western cultures, and newcomers often misread it. *อายุเท่าไหร่* isn't an attempt to judge you; it's an attempt to find the right form of address. Answer honestly — and if you'd rather not, *เดาสิคะ/ครับ dao sì* ("take a guess") is accepted with a laugh.
**อายุ aa-yú means age, and the number STANDS ALONE without the word "years".** *อายุสามสิบสอง* = thirty-two years old. Adding *ปี pii* isn't wrong, just unnecessary.

**Nicknames (ชื่อเล่น chûue-lên) are used far more than real names.** Almost every Thai has a one-syllable nickname — *นก* (bird), *ต้น* (tree), *เบียร์* (beer), *เอ* (A) — and that's what's used at work, at school, even in formal meetings. Real Thai names can be five syllables long and usually appear only on documents.
**คุณ khun before a name is the safest form for someone new.** *คุณนก* = Ms. Nok. Once you're on friendly terms, people switch to *พี่นก* or *น้องนก* depending on age.

**จะได้ jà dâai means "so that".** *ต้องรู้อายุก่อน จะได้รู้ว่าเรียกพี่หรือน้อง* = we need to know your age first, so that we know what to call you. This pattern is very often used to explain a purpose.
**เรียก rîak means "to call, address".** *เรียกผมว่าบูดีก็ได้ครับ rîak phǒm wâa Buu-dii kâw dâai khráp* = just call me Budi. A very useful sentence when introducing yourself.

after: ⚠️ **Grandparents are distinguished by WHICH SIDE of the family**: *ปู่/ย่า* on your father's side, *ตา/ยาย* on your mother's side. English doesn't make this distinction, and Thais consider it as important as telling father from mother.

⚠️ **แฟน faaen comes from the English word *fan* but means a boyfriend, girlfriend, or steady partner** — not a fan. *มีแฟนหรือยัง mii faaen rǔue yang* ("do you have a boyfriend/girlfriend yet?") is one of the questions you'll be asked most often.

grammars.title: Personal questions you'll be asked, and how to answer them
body: These questions often come up in the first ten minutes of meeting someone. All of them count as friendly, not nosy.

after: **…หรือยัง *rǔue yang* means "…yet?"** and there are only two answers: *แล้ว láaeo* (yes, already) or *ยัง yang* (not yet). This pattern comes back in Unit 11 and works for anything: *กินข้าวหรือยัง* (have you eaten yet?), *ถึงหรือยัง* (are you there yet?).

If you don't want to answer, the polite way out isn't refusing but smiling and deflecting: *เป็นความลับครับ/ค่ะ pen khwaam-láp* — "it's a secret". Said with a laugh, it's accepted without any problem.

blocks.text: Thai has no neutral "sir" or "ma'am" that fits everyone — what it has are terms that place people on an age map. This list will save you in almost every situation.

head: Term
Pronunciation
For whom
rows: someone who looks older than you
someone who looks younger; servers, cashiers
people your parents' age — warm, familiar
คุณลุง / คุณป้า
a more polite version of the above
a middle-aged woman vendor — very common at markets
a small child; also used by girls to refer to themselves
ครู / อาจารย์
teachers and lecturers — addressed by their title

blocks.title: If you guess the age wrong
items: Calling someone *พี่* who turns out to be younger is **perfectly fine** — it sounds respectful.
⚠️ Calling someone *น้อง* who turns out to be older **feels a bit off**. When in doubt, always choose *พี่*. It's a practical rule that never backfires.
For restaurant servers, the most common form of address is *น้อง* followed by *ครับ/ค่ะ* — or simply raising your hand. Don't snap your fingers or whistle; that's considered rude everywhere.

sections.title: Describing your family in five sentences

blocks.text: You can use this pattern as is; just swap in your own numbers.

items: **ครอบครัวผม/ฉันมีห้าคนครับ/ค่ะ** — there are five people in my family.
**มีพ่อ แม่ พี่ชาย และน้องสาวครับ/ค่ะ** — my father, my mother, an older brother, and a younger sister.
**พ่อเป็นครู แม่เป็นแม่บ้านครับ/ค่ะ** — my father is a teacher, my mother is a homemaker.
**ผม/ฉันอายุสามสิบสองครับ/ค่ะ** — I'm thirty-two.
**ยังไม่ได้แต่งงานครับ/ค่ะ** — I'm not married yet.

blocks.title: One thing to know about Thai families
items: A child's duty to their parents — called *กตัญญู kà-tan-yuu* — is a very strong value in Thailand, and it's more than a feeling: many young people send a large part of their salary home every month, and that's considered normal, not a sacrifice.

So the question *ส่งเงินให้ที่บ้านไหม sòng ngoen hâi thîi bâan mǎi* ("do you send money home?") can come up in ordinary conversation. It isn't a question about your money; it's a question about your relationship with your family.
